facts.claim: "Cannibal Within" was released on October 6, 2023 on Liars Club Records.
The song is self-produced and was recorded in a backwoods bar that had been turned into a studio.
The track is banjo-driven. Its experimental percussion includes a repeatedly dropped pick, bottle tinks and clacking toy teeth.
It is the lead single from Amigo the Devil's third studio album, Yours Until the War Is Over, which was announced for release on February 23, 2024.

Danny Kiranos said there is a tiny cannibal inside everyone that feeds on insecurities. He said the more it feeds on doubt, jealousy and self-devaluation, the bigger it grows, until we are left with nothing and lose the war.

Kiranos told Spin the song was originally conceived as a meditation on the harmful ways people try to counter aging. It went from being "pompous" (his word) to one of the album's most powerful statements on regret.
Here Comes The Flood describes the song as being about death, addiction, depression and fentanyl. The lyrics include a Hotel California reference.
An official lyric video was shot and directed by Natasha Austrich, with animations by Disembodied.
In a 2025 interview, Kiranos said the cannibal within encompasses self-doubt and jealousy that come from allowing himself to be constantly uncertain, and that it "just grows and grows and grows."
Amigo the Devil is the stage name of Danny Kiranos, an American singer-songwriter, guitarist and banjo player born in Miami, Florida in 1987. He took the name while living in San Francisco.

research.lineage: Press places the song in dark folk and alternative Americana, a murder-folk tradition whose biggest influences Kiranos is said to share with Tom Waits and Leonard Cohen.

draft:
The joke that lands hardest in **Cannibal Within** is a suicide joke. The verse opens by announcing, almost like a weather report, that it turns out the narrator is depressed. Then it offers a fix: turn on the radio, cock it back. Then comes the caveat: "I just don't wanna blow my brains out to Hotel California." It's funny, and it's meant to be. But a line earlier the song told you what the funny is for. Someone has noticed that this person uses jokes and joy to dodge the realization. The narrator hears the diagnosis and answers it with another joke. That's the trap, shown in one move.

The opening verse works the same way. The narrator always figured the great fear would be heartbreak, "Be love related, not fentanyl." There's embarrassment in that line, a life that was supposed to go wrong in a more romantic direction. What follows is the addict's loop told without self-pity: a heart beating off its rhythm, a vow to every god that this is the last time, and then the admission, before anyone else can say it, that everybody knows it's a lie. Shame and plain honesty sit side by side, and neither wins.

Then the chorus does something quietly generous. It trades "I" for "we." The parts we hate pile up "Until we find ourselves with more regret than blood," and the title's cannibal stops being one person's problem. Danny Kiranos, the Miami-born songwriter behind the name, has described a tiny cannibal inside everyone that feeds on doubt, jealousy and self-devaluation and grows until we lose the war. The word matters, since this was the lead single from his third album, *Yours Until the War Is Over*. He told Spin the song began as a meditation on the harmful ways people fight aging, an idea he called "pompous," before it became one of the record's heaviest statements on regret.

The sound refuses to match the panic. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios over a walking bass. The tempo is slow and steady, and everything is dry and close, as if the room were small. Kiranos self-produced it in a backwoods bar turned studio, and that intimacy holds. The voice sits low-to-mid and a little raspy, carrying the melody with no harmony to lean on. This is dark folk out of the murder-folk tradition, drawing on influences Kiranos shares with Tom Waits and Leonard Cohen, and here the killer and the victim are the same person. The verse about the sea and the heart as a lonely hunter lets the jokes fall silent for a moment, and the song is at its bravest there.

It sticks because the punchline and the confession arrive in the same breath, so you laugh first and only then realize you've been shown how someone keeps going one more day.
